extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 19th-century domestic fiction / literary readers
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter from a 19th-century domestic novel about visiting, household life, manners, dress, and a village party; useful for readers or scholars studying social norms and etiquette in period fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calls and visiting etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls and Visiting (chapter theme): social expectations around calling, receiving visitors, and informal visits in a small community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual guidance and examples: callers often 'run in' for a short time; visits may include staying to supper ("she had got to stay and see Richard; besides that, they were going to have waffles and honey"); people are expected to call on newcomers; invitations are broadly extended (from clergy down to dressmakers) and returning calls is implied. Anti-pattern: failing to receive or return visits leads to gossip or suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate dress for occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Dress should fit local standards of modesty and occasion; what is fashionable in one place may be 'out of place' elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ethelyn decides not to wear white satin because it would be 'out of place'; Richard thinks her dress 'too low' and Mrs. Markham complains about exposed shoulderblades and long trains. Guidance implies matching attire to community norms (modest necklines, sensible skirt lengths) and that overt fashion can be criticized by local elders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host provision of refreshments and hospitality
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful visit or party requires substantial and appropriate refreshments and visible hospitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of expected fare: waffles and honey, warm gingerbread, Charlotte Russe, blanc-mange, tarts, jellies, raised biscuits, frosted cakes, and frozen desserts (iced pail stirred by family). 'The waffles and the gingerbread were all they had promised to be' signals that good food meets social expectations. Practical note: table laid in the kitchen, with head waiter and attendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic neatness and room presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rooms, hearths, and domestic spaces should be clean and presented attractively for guests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and actions: sweeping, dusting, patting pillows; washing the hearth with milk to give bricks a polished appearance; kitchen floor cleared up before visitors. Guidance: attention to small domestic details increases cheerfulness and makes a good impression on guests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of household labor and role expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations about who performs chores (mistress vs hired help) and which tasks are appropriate for different social positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mrs. Markham expects Ethelyn should not do chores, preferring Eunice to remain; 'it struck her as perfectly proper that one like Ethelyn should sit still while others served.' Guidance: class- and role-based norms dictate whether a young wife participates in ironing, dish-washing, etc.; refusing or accepting such roles affects family dynamics and community perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match music/entertainment to audience tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances at social gatherings should consider the audience's familiarity and taste; highbrow displays can alienate a local crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Ethelyn plays a brilliant, difficult overture and is praised for skill, but listeners want 'something familiar' and Tim asks 'give us a tune.' Guidance: prefer accessible, familiar pieces when entertaining a broad, local assembly; virtuosity may be admired by some but unwelcome by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical party organization and logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize physical space and logistics to suit the planned activities (dancing, dining, serving).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete measures in text: remove bed from sitting room and take up carpet to make room for dancing; use lamp and candle lighting (kerosene, sperm, tallow) appropriate for rooms; set table in kitchen and assign head waiter; ice and tubs for frozen desserts. Guidance: attention to these practical steps is necessary to run a successful village party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness, unpretentiousness, and community reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Social warmth and modest behavior are valued and can have practical consequences for family status or ambitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Melinda advises that 'a little attention, which cost nothing, would go a great ways' to help Richard's potential political prospects; townspeople excuse initial pride as homesickness but expect the bride to 'unbend.' Guidance: adapting one's demeanour to be polite and approachable strengthens social bonds and can support public ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local informality vs Eastern propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: Prairie/community manners may be more informal than Eastern 'Mrs. Grundy' standards; visitors should expect different social rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted contrast: 'on the prairie they were not hampered with many of Mrs. Grundy's rules.' Guidance: newcomers should anticipate more casual timing and approaches to calling and hospitality in the Western setting; being rigidly formal may be misunderstood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to clothing maintenance and mending
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper mending, ironing, and care of garments (including children's clothing) are part of respectable household conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mrs. Markham patching Andy's pants; discussion of ironing puffs, embroidery, and ruffles; Eunice's careful washing and starching. Guidance: visible care in mending and laundering signals thrift, propriety, and competence; neglect or improper care invites criticism.
